payload.text:
Short answer: the cut-outs are most likely two deterministic bugs in the app's own controller plumbing, not the iPad running out of headroom. And no, there is nothing today that records input timing, so latency itself cannot be tracked from the current build.

**How a stick reaches Dolphin** (I traced the full chain, including the two submodules that aren't checked out in this worktree, by fetching the exact commits the `jit-spike` build pins):

1. GameController HID callbacks land in DeltaCore's `MFiGameController` on a dedicated off-main queue. Each axis change becomes "deactivate the opposite direction, activate this direction with a value".
2. Stick samples go through DeltaCore's `AnalogInputCoalescer`, which keeps the last sample per input and flushes them all to the main thread once per run-loop pass.
3. On main, `NGCEmulatorBridge` in `ManicEmu/ManicEmu/Sources/Tools/Cores/NGC.swift` turns the direction values back into an (x, y) point and calls RetroArch's stick setter for that player.
4. RetroArch's `manic_joypad` driver stores it in per-port arrays. Dolphin reads them once per frame. The whole Dolphin frame also runs on the main thread, driven by a CADisplayLink.

**Bug 1, stick state shared across players** (`NGC.swift:123-124`). The bridge is a singleton with one `leftThumbstickPosition` and one `rightThumbstickPosition` for everyone. When player 2 pushes right, the bridge sends player 2's x together with whatever y player 1 last set. When player 1 lets go, the component is zeroed and sent for player 1, and player 2's held deflection is now gone from the shared state too. That is exactly "both sticks at once, each controller cuts out". It only shows with two or more controllers, which is why single-player feels fine. Upstream Manic EMU has the same code, and the Wii, N64, PS1, DOS, Arcade, Amiga and C64 bridges share the pattern.

**Bug 2, unordered flush.** The coalescer flushes a Swift dictionary, so a flick through center within one busy frame can deliver "activate right" before "deactivate left", leaving the stick at zero while it's held hard over until the player wiggles it. Longer Dolphin frames batch more events per flush, so a loaded minigame makes this more frequent, but it's a frontend bug, not a performance limit.

**Is the iPad being pushed too far?** Not by these symptoms. An M4 iPad Air is far from GameCube's ceiling with JIT on. Without JIT the interpreter runs at a reduced clock and frames can exceed 16 ms, which adds one frame of input delay through the main-thread hop above, but it would degrade smoothly rather than make a held stick read zero. The session log in `Documents/Netplay Logs/Manic MP sessions.log` says which mode each session ran in, so you can check whether JIT was actually on during that Mario Party session.

**Observability today:**

- Every Dolphin launch on the installed build writes a RetroArch INFO log plus one run-mode line. Useful for "was JIT on", nothing more.
- Frame-time stats exist only inside a connected netplay session.
- No input event is ever timestamped. Nothing reads Apple's per-controller `lastEventLatency`, nothing measures the hop to main, and the app's own debug logging is compiled out of release builds.
- Also noted: audio latency is set to 200 ms at launch, which adds perceived lag without causing drop-outs.

I saved the traced path and both bugs to the shared Track memory. The card above offers two next steps: fix the per-player state and ordered flush (the likely cure), and add input timing to the session log so the remaining latency can be measured rather than guessed.

Sources: [Apple, Handling input events](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/gamecontroller/handling-input-events), [Apple, lastEventTimestamp](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/gamecontroller/gcphysicalinputprofile/lasteventtimestamp)

The iPad never needs to touch the Mac, but the Mac is still needed for the compile. That pipeline is already built and running on the Pi. A new build takes three steps.

1. **Build on the Mac.** Xcode is the only thing that can compile it. RetroArch and DeltaCore are submodules of the Manic project, so one Xcode build of the Sideload scheme compiles all of it together. The iPad does not have to be plugged in or even nearby.
2. **Hand the build to the Pi.** On the Mac, run `mac-export-manic.sh` from the better-games `signer/` folder. It picks the newest device build out of Xcode's build folder, zips it, and copies it to the Pi signer's inbox over SSH. Nothing is signed on the Mac.
3. **The Pi signs and installs it.** Run this on the Pi, or ask me to:

```sh
~/.local/share/ios-signer/scripts/resign.sh ~/.local/share/ios-signer/inbox/manic.ipa com.globocodes.manicemu
```

It re-signs with your Apple ID session, checks the bundle id, team and JIT entitlement, then upgrades the app on the iPad over the tailnet or home Wi-Fi.

Three things to know about the current state:

- **The hourly timer will not pick up a new build by itself.** It only re-signs when an app has under three days of signing left. Manic is good until October 6, so it is skipping. A new build needs the manual command in step 3.
- **The Pi's copy is stale.** The build in its inbox is from September 29, before the stick fix. If you skip step 2, the next scheduled re-sign reinstalls that old copy over whatever is on the iPad.
- **The iPad has to be reachable.** It must be awake, and LocalDevVPN must be off during the install because it takes over the VPN slot from Tailscale. On the home network the Pi falls back to the LAN address.

For the stick fix specifically, step 1 also includes the merge into `jit-spike` and the submodule update. Those commands are in the runbook "Two controllers move independently in Mario Party 4 on the iPad".

The only way to drop the Mac entirely would be a hosted macOS build runner feeding the Pi's inbox. You chose on September 29 to keep builds on the Mac, so I have not set that up.
